## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.94070.3.sa2](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.94070.3.sa2)

In Bing et al, the authors analyze micro-C data from NC14 fly embryos, focusing on the eve locus, to assess different models of chromatin looping. They conclude that fly TADs are less consistent with conventional cohesin-based loop extrusion models and instead rely more heavily on boundary-boundary pairings in an orientation-dependent manner.

Overall, I found the manuscript to be interesting and thought-provoking. However, this paper reads much more like a perspective than a research article. Considering the journal is aimed at the general audience, I strongly suggest the authors spend some time editing their introduction to the most salient points as well as organizing their results section in a more conventional way with conclusion-based titles. It was very difficult to follow the authors' logic throughout the manuscript as written. It was also not clear as written which experiments were performed as part of this study and which were reanalyzed but published elsewhere. This should be made clearer throughout.

It has been shown several times that Drosophila Hi-C maps do not contain all of the features (frequent corner peaks, stripes, etc.) observed when compared to mammalian cells. Considering these features are thought to be products of extrusion events, it is not an entirely new concept that Drosophila domains form via mechanisms other than extrusion. That being said, the authors' analyses do not distinguish between the formation and the maintenance of domains. It is not clear to this reviewer why a single mechanism should explain the formation of the complex structures observed in static Hi-C heatmaps from a population of cells at a single developmental time point. For example, how can the authors rule out that extrusion initially provides the necessary proximity and possibly the cis preference of contacts required for boundary-boundary pairing whereas the latter may more reflect the structures observed at maintenance? Future work aimed at analyzing micro-C data in cohesin-depleted cells might shed additional light on this.

Additional mechanisms at play include compartment-level interactions driven by chromatin states. Indeed, in mammalian cells, these interactions often manifest as a "plume" on Hi-C maps similar to what the authors attribute to boundary interactions in this manuscript. How do the chromatin states in the neighboring domains of the eve locus impact the model if at all?

How does intrachromosomal homolog pairing impact the models proposed in this manuscript (Abed et al. 2019; Erceg et al., 2019). Several papers recently have shown that somatic homolog pairing is not uniform and shows significant variation across the genome with evidence for both tight pairing regions and loose pairing regions. Might loose pairing interactions have the capacity to alter the cis configuration of the eve locus?

In summary, the transgenic experiments are extensive and elegant and fully support the authors' models. However, in my opinion, they do not completely rule out additional models at play, including extrusion-based mechanisms. Indeed, my major issue is the limited conceptual advance in this manuscript. The authors essentially repeat many of their previous work and analyses. The authors make no attempt to dissect the mechanism of this process by modifying extrusion components directly. Some discussion of Rollins et al., 1999 on the discovery of Nipped-B and its role in enhancer-promoter communication should also be made to reconcile their conclusions in the proposed absence of extrusion events.

## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.94070.3.sa3](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.94070.3.sa3)

Bing et al. attempt to address fundamental mechanisms of TAD formation in Drosophila by analyzing gene expression and 3D conformation within the vicinity of the eve TAD after insertion of a transgene harboring a Homie insulator sequence 142 kb away in different orientations. These transgenes along with spatial gene expression analysis were previously published in Fujioka et al. 2016, and the underlying interpretations regarding resulting DNA configuration in this genomic region were also previously published. This manuscript repeats the expression analysis using smFISH probes in order to achieve more quantitative analysis, but the main results are the same as previously published. The only new data are the Micro-C and an additional modeling/analysis of what they refer to as the 'Z3' orientation of the transgenes. The rest of the manuscript merely synthesizes further interpretation with the goal of addressing whether loop extrusion may be occurring or if boundary:boundary pairing without loop extrusion is responsible for TAD formation. The authors conclude that their results are more consistent with boundary:boundary pairing and not loop extrusion; however, most of this imaging data seems to support both loop extrusion and the boundary:boundary models. This manuscript lacks support, especially new data, for its conclusions. Furthermore, there are many parts of the manuscript that are difficult to follow. There are some minor errors in the labelling of the figures that if fixed would help elevate understanding. Lastly, there are several major points that if elaborated on, would potentially be helpful for the clarity of the manuscript.

Major Points:

(1) The authors suggest and attempt to visualize in the supplemental figures, that loop extrusion mechanisms would appear during crosslinking and show as vertical stripes in the micro-C data. In order to see stripes, a majority of the nuclei would need to undergo loop extrusion at the same rate, starting from exactly the same spots, and the loops would also have to be released and restarted at the same rate. If these patterns truly result from loop extrusion, the authors should provide experimental evidence from another organism undergoing loop extrusion.

(2) On lines 311-314, the authors discuss that stem-loops generated by cohesin extrusion would possibly be expected to have more next-next-door neighbor contacts than next-door neighbor contacts and site their models in Figure 1. Based on the boundary:boundary pairing models in the same figure would the stem-loops created by head-to-tail pairing also have the same phenotype? Making possible enrichment of next-next-door neighbor contacts possible in both situations? The concepts in the text are not clear, and the diagrams are not well-labeled relative to the two models.

(3) The authors appear to cite Chen et al., 2018 as a reference for the location of these transgenes being 700nM away in a majority of the nuclei. However, the exact transgenes in this manuscript do not appear to have been measured for distance. The authors could do this experiment and include expression measurements.

(4) The authors discuss the possible importance of CTCF orientation in forming the roadblock to cohesin extrusion and discuss that Homie orientation in the transgene may impact Homie function as an effective roadblock. However, the Homie region inserted in the transgene does not contain the CTCF motif. Can the authors elaborate on why they feel the orientation of Homie is important in its ability to function as a roadblock if the CTCF motif is not present? Trans-acting factors responsible for Homie function have not been identified and this point is not discussed in the manuscript.

(5) The imaging results seem to be consistent with both boundary:boundary interaction and loop extrusion stem looping.

(6) The authors suggest that the eveMa TAD could only be formed by extrusion after the breakthrough of Nhomie and several other roadblocks. Additionally, the overall long-range interactions with Nhomie appear to be less than the interactions with endogenous Homie (Figures 7, 8, and supplemental 5). Is it possible that in some cases boundary:boundary pairing is occurring between only the transgenic Homie and endogenous Homie and not including Nhomie?

(7) In Figure 4E, the GFP hebe expression shown in the LhomieG Z5 transgenic embryo does not appear in the same locations as the LlambdaG Z5 control. Is this actually hebe expression or just a background signal?

(8) Figure 6- The LhomieG Z3 late-stage embryo appears to be showing the ventral orientation of the embryo rather than the lateral side of the embryo as was shown in the previous figure. Is this for a reason? Additionally, there are no statistics shown for the Z3 transgenic images. Were these images analyzed in the same way as the Z5 line images?

(9) Do the Micro-C data align with the developmental time points used in the smFISH probe assays?

claims.evidence: This describes the mechanism of the loop-extrusion model.

claims.claim: In the loop-extrusion model, the location of roadblocks combined with the processive action of the cohesin complex determines the endpoints of each TAD.
claims.source: The location of these roadblocks combined with the processive action of the cohesin complex determines the endpoints of each TAD (Davidson and Peters, 2021; Ghosh and Meyer, 2021; Mirny and Dekker, 2022; Perea-Resa et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This describes a key feature of the loop-extrusion model, supported by citations.

claims.claim: A key assumption of the loop-extrusion model is that mammalian boundaries are fully autonomous.
claims.source: A key assumption of the loop-extrusion model is that mammalian boundaries are fully autonomous: they are roadblocks, and their physical presence in and of itself is sufficient to define the loop endpoint, independent of the functional properties of neighboring boundaries.
claims.evidence: This describes a fundamental assumption of the loop-extrusion model.

claims.claim: In a variant of the loop-extrusion model, the relative orientation of the paired CTCF roadblocks is important for halting cohesin-mediated extrusion.
claims.source: In a more specific variant of this model, the relative orientation of the paired CTCF roadblocks is also important—in order to halt cohesin-mediated extrusion, the CTCF sites on each side of the loop must have a convergent orientation.
claims.evidence: This describes a specific variant of the loop-extrusion model.

claims.claim: In the orientation-dependent variant of the loop-extrusion model, CTCF roadblocks can block an oncoming cohesin complex in only one direction.
claims.source: In this model, the CTCF roadblocks are able to block an oncoming cohesin complex in only one direction; however, their intrinsic blocking activity is independent of the orientation of other CTCF sites in their neighborhood.
claims.evidence: This describes a feature of the orientation-dependent loop-extrusion model.

claims.claim: The evidence regarding TAD formation and function in flies is seemingly inconsistent with the loop-extrusion mechanism.
claims.source: While this loop-extrusion mechanism is widely thought to be operative in mammals, the evidence regarding TAD formation and function in flies is seemingly inconsistent with this mechanism.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the state of evidence in the field.

claims.claim: Genetics studies have shown that fly boundaries are functionally non-autonomous.
claims.source: Genetics studies have shown that fly boundaries are functionally non-autonomous and that their activities in both loop formation and gene regulation depend upon their ability to engage in direct physical interactions with other boundaries (Chetverina et al., 2014; Chetverina et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to genetic studies.

claims.claim: The activities of fly boundaries in both loop formation and gene regulation depend upon their ability to engage in direct physical interactions with other boundaries.
claims.source: Genetics studies have shown that fly boundaries are functionally non-autonomous and that their activities in both loop formation and gene regulation depend upon their ability to engage in direct physical interactions with other boundaries (Chetverina et al., 2014; Chetverina et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to genetic studies.

claims.claim: The gypsy transposon su(Hw) boundary can mediate regulatory interactions between transgenes inserted at sites separated by 15–32 Mb or more.
claims.source: That fly boundaries might function by physical pairing was first suggested by studies which showed that the gypsy transposon su(Hw) boundary and the bithorax complex (BX-C) Mcp boundary can mediate regulatory interactions (enhancer/silencer: reporter) between transgenes inserted at sites separated by 15–32 Mb or more (Muller et al., 1999; Sigrist and Pirrotta, 1997; Vazquez et al., 1993).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claims.claim: The bithorax complex (BX-C) Mcp boundary can mediate regulatory interactions between transgenes inserted at sites separated by 15–32 Mb or more.
claims.source: That fly boundaries might function by physical pairing was first suggested by studies which showed that the gypsy transposon su(Hw) boundary and the bithorax complex (BX-C) Mcp boundary can mediate regulatory interactions (enhancer/silencer: reporter) between transgenes inserted at sites separated by 15–32 Mb or more (Muller et al., 1999; Sigrist and Pirrotta, 1997; Vazquez et al., 1993).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claims.claim: Distant transgenes containing the same boundary co-localize in vivo and remain in contact for extended periods of time.
claims.source: Consistent with direct physical interactions, these distant transgenes co-localize in vivo, and in living tissue remain in contact for extended periods of time (Chen et al., 2018; Li et al., 2011; Vazquez et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to imaging studies.

claims.source: However, if the same boundary is placed downstream of the closest reporter, bypass is observed. In this case the closest reporter, which is bracketed by the two boundaries, is still insulated from the enhancers; however, the downstream reporter is activated (Muravyova et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: This describes the results of the bypass assay, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Bypass activity is, in most cases, orientation-dependent.
claims.source: Kyrchanova et al., 2008a showed that bypass activity is, in most cases, orientation-dependent.

claims.source: When the same boundary is placed in the upstream and downstream position, they typically need to be introduced in the opposite orientation.

claims.claim: One feature of the eve TAD is inconsistent with the loop-extrusion model: there are no vertical stripes or 45° stripes that would be expected from loop extrusion intermediates.
claims.source: While a stem-loop is the topology expected for the eve TAD in both models, one feature of the TAD is inconsistent with the loop-extrusion model. According to this model, loops (TADs) are generated by a cohesin complex that forms a small bubble at a loading site somewhere in the TAD-to-be and then extrudes both strands of the growing loop at an equal rate until it bumps into the boundary roadblocks (Davidson and Peters, 2021; Ghosh and Meyer, 2021; Mirny and Dekker, 2022; Perea-Resa et al., 2021). If the loading site were located in the middle of the TAD-to-be, and the extrusion intermediates in a population of nuclei were captured by crosslinking, one should observe a crosslink-generated stripe that begins at the loading site and extends perpendicular to the chromosomal DNA until it reaches the apex that links the two TAD boundaries with imaginary lines of 45° (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B). This is the pattern that would be generated by a 'broken zipper' when it transiently links the zipper teeth equidistant from the initial 'loading site' (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A). If the loading site is off center to the left, the crosslinking of the passing cohesin complex in a population of nuclei will generate a perpendicular stripe until cohesin come to a halt when it encounters the roadblock on the left (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C). Assuming that the complex continues to extrude the right strand, it will then generate a stripe at a 45° angle that extends to the apex of the TAD. If the loading site corresponds to one of the CTCF roadblocks or is located close to the roadblock, the cohesin complex will generate a 45° stripe that comes to a halt at the apex of the triangle when it encounters the neighboring CTCF roadblock (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D and E). If there are multiple loading sites within the TAD, there should be a series of perpendicular stripes that generate and sequentially reinforce the stripe(s) at 45° (Figure 2—figure supplement 2F). However, in spite of the fact that NC14 fly embryos should provide by far the best prospect of actually capturing loop extrusion intermediates, there are no vertical stripes in the eve TAD, nor are there stripes at 45° that extend to the apex of the eve TAD. Nor do we observe a population of perpendicular stripes that convert into a series of reinforced 45° stripes. There is also no evidence of stripes that are initially tilted to the left or right of a 'loading site', as might be observed if the rate of extrusion were unequal on the two strands, and then subsequently convert to a 45° stripe as cohesin comes to a halt at the first boundary encountered.
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of the MicroC data and comparison to theoretical predictions illustrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

results.result: Two competing models exist for TAD formation: the loop-extrusion model where cohesin extrudes loops until encountering autonomous boundary roadblocks (generating only stem-loops and unanchored loops), and the boundary-pairing model where non-autonomous boundaries physically pair with partners (generating both stem-loops and circle-loops).
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C7 accurately describe established knowledge about the two competing models for TAD formation, as evidenced by extensive citations throughout the manuscript. The key distinguishing features (boundary autonomy, loop topologies) are well-documented in the literature.

results.result: Using MicroC analysis and experimental manipulation of the homie boundary, the authors conclude that TAD formation in flies is incompatible with loop-extrusion and instead occurs through boundary-pairing mechanisms that do not require loop extrusion.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C12 and C169 represent the main conclusion of the study. The experimental approach (MicroC + transgene manipulations) is clearly described, and the conclusion is supported by multiple lines of evidence presented throughout the results section, including absence of expected loop-extrusion signatures and presence of orientation-dependent pairing interactions.

results.result: The eve TAD is defined by nhomie and homie boundaries, forms a stem-loop structure with a volcano plume, and exhibits high internal contact density consistent with boundary-pairing bringing flanking sequences into proximity.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C85 describe the basic architecture of the eve TAD as observed in MicroC data (Figure 2A-B). The stem-loop topology is inferred from the volcano plume pattern, which is consistent with both models. The interpretation is supported by previous transgene studies showing that stem-loops enable enhancer-reporter bypass.

results.result: The eve TAD lacks vertical or 45° crosslinking stripes that would be expected from loop-extrusion intermediates, inconsistent with the loop-extrusion model.
results.evaluation: Claim C86 presents a critical negative result. The absence of expected loop-extrusion signatures (perpendicular and 45° stripes) in NC14 embryos—which should be optimal for capturing such intermediates—is clearly documented in the MicroC data and extensively discussed with reference to theoretical predictions (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).

results.result: The chromosomal region between the -142 kb attP site and eve contains at least 10 distinct TADs (TC-TL) whose endpoints correspond to sequences bound by known architectural factors, representing fundamental building blocks of 3D chromosome organization.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C91 describe the TAD organization between the transgene insertion site and eve locus as observed in MicroC data (Figure 2C). The correlation between TAD endpoints and ChIP-seq peaks for architectural proteins provides strong support for these being functional boundaries.

results.result: Superimposed on the TADs between hebe and eve are lower-density contact (LDC) domains linking neighboring TADs, though the eve TAD interacts less frequently with its neighbors than other TADs in the region.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C95 describe the hierarchical organization of LDC domains observed in MicroC data (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1). The observation that eve TAD shows reduced inter-TAD contacts compared to neighboring TADs is clearly documented and relevant for distinguishing between models.

results.result: TADs between eve and the attP site are defined by volcano triangles without plumes, surrounded by LDC clouds, and lack perpendicular or angled crosslinking stripes expected from loop extrusion.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C99 describe key features of TADs in the eve neighborhood that distinguish them from expectations of the loop-extrusion model. The absence of volcano plumes and crosslinking stripes is clearly documented in the MicroC data and represents important negative evidence against loop extrusion.

results.result: While the loop-extrusion model would explain LDC domains through boundary breakthrough events, there is no evidence of expected 45° crosslinking stripes, and nhomie does not appear particularly prone to breakthrough despite the presence of LDC domains.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C103 present a critical test of the loop-extrusion model. The absence of 45° stripes that should mark breakthrough events, combined with the observation that eve TAD is less frequently incorporated into LDC domains, provides strong evidence against the loop-extrusion explanation for LDC domains.

results.result: In the boundary-pairing model, LDC domains could arise from proximity-based crosslinking between neighboring circle-loop TADs or from switching/combining pairing partners, consistent with pairing interactions being long-duration but not permanent.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C106 propose alternative mechanisms for LDC domain formation in the boundary-pairing model. While these are plausible explanations supported by imaging studies showing transient pairing (C106), they remain speculative interpretations (Figure 2—figure supplement 3) that require additional experimental validation.

results.result: A minimal 367 bp homie fragment lacking CTCF but containing other boundary protein sites can mediate regulatory interactions between eve enhancers and reporters at -142 kb, with partial activation at blastoderm stage and more complete activation during mid-embryogenesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C113 describe previous findings (Fujioka et al., 2016) that establish the experimental system. The composition of the minimal homie fragment and the stage-specific activation patterns are well-documented and provide important context for the current experiments.

results.result: Live imaging shows that in blastoderm embryos, the majority of nuclei (~80-85%) do not express the transgene reporter and maintain ~700 nM distance from eve, while the expressing subset maintains closer proximity (~330 nM) for extended periods (~30 min).
results.evaluation: Claims C114-C117 cite live imaging data (Chen et al., 2018) showing correlation between physical proximity and transcriptional activation. These findings support the boundary-pairing model by demonstrating that long-distance activation requires sustained physical contact.

results.result: The boundary-pairing and loop-extrusion models make different predictions for how the transgene at -142 kb interacts with eve: pairing predicts looping over intervening TADs to pair with nhomie/homie, while extrusion requires breakthrough of multiple boundaries to form an eveMammoth TAD.
results.evaluation: Claims C118-C120 clearly articulate the competing predictions of the two models (illustrated in Figure 3). These predictions form the basis for the experimental tests and are logically derived from the fundamental mechanisms of each model.

results.result: The GlambdaL control transgene (lacking homie) shows no eve-dependent reporter expression at blastoderm stage, with later expression driven by hebe enhancers in a dorsal midline pattern.
results.evaluation: Claims C121-C123 describe the negative control showing that without homie, there is no long-distance activation by eve enhancers (Figure 4C, E). This establishes that the boundary element is required for the observed regulatory interactions.

results.result: In the GeimohL transgene (homie pointing away from eve), eve-lacZ is expressed in an eve pattern (7 stripes at blastoderm, mesoderm/CNS/anal plate later), while eve-gfp is not activated by eve enhancers but is expressed in midline under hebe enhancer control.
results.evaluation: Claims C124-C129 describe the expression patterns for GeimohL (Figure 4C, E), showing orientation-dependent activation where only the reporter upstream of homie (eve-lacZ) responds to eve enhancers. This is consistent with both models' predictions for this configuration.

results.result: In the GhomieL transgene (homie pointing toward eve), eve-gfp is activated by both eve and hebe enhancers while eve-lacZ is insulated from both, supporting the boundary-pairing model's prediction of circle-loop formation but contradicting the loop-extrusion model.
results.evaluation: Claims C130-C135 present the critical test distinguishing the models (Figure 5). The switch in which reporter is activated when homie orientation is reversed, combined with the dual activation of eve-gfp, strongly supports boundary-pairing (which can form circle-loops) over loop-extrusion (which cannot).

results.result: In LeimohG and LhomieG transgenes (opposite chromosomal orientation), the reporter activated by eve enhancers switches based on homie orientation within the transgene, with LeimohG activating eve-gfp and LhomieG activating eve-lacZ.
results.evaluation: Claims C136-C141 demonstrate that the orientation of homie within the transgene, not the transgene's chromosomal orientation, determines which reporter is activated (Figure 6F, G). This confirms the orientation-dependence of boundary pairing and rules out simple distance effects.

results.result: The GlambdaL control shows weak but detectable physical interaction with the eve locus (likely mediated by eve promoters), though this interaction is insufficient to drive reporter expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C142-C144 describe an unexpected finding in the MicroC data (Figure 7A). While the interaction is weak and functionally insufficient, its presence suggests that promoter-mediated contacts may occur independently of boundary-mediated pairing. The speculation about promoters (C144) is appropriately qualified.

results.result: In GeimohL, strong crosslinking between the transgene and eve TAD parallels reporter activation, with preferential interaction of eve-lacZ (vs eve-gfp) with sequences across the eve TAD.
results.evaluation: Claims C145-C148 show that physical interactions detected by MicroC (Figure 7B) correlate with functional activation patterns, with the activated reporter (eve-lacZ) showing stronger interactions with eve sequences than the inactive reporter (eve-gfp), as confirmed by virtual 4C analysis (Figure 7D).

results.result: In GeimohL, there is no evidence of cohesin breaking through multiple boundaries to form eveMammoth TAD, no disruption of the eve TAD structure, and no novel vertical/45° crosslinking stripes expected from loop extrusion.
results.evaluation: Claims C149-C151 present critical negative evidence against the loop-extrusion model. The preservation of intervening TAD organization and the intact eve TAD structure (Figure 7B), combined with absence of expected crosslinking signatures, strongly argue against the breakthrough mechanism required by loop extrusion.

results.result: In GeimohL, the transgene homie interacts with both endogenous homie and nhomie, with stronger self-pairing than heterologous pairing, suggesting the transgene pairs with both boundaries in a pattern that maintains the intact eve TAD.
results.evaluation: Claims C152-C154 describe virtual 4C results (Figure 8A) showing dual interactions consistent with the boundary-pairing model. The stronger self-pairing is consistent with known pairing preferences, and the inference about simultaneous pairing (C154) is reasonable given the intact eve TAD.

results.result: In GhomieL (reversed homie), eve-gfp rather than eve-lacZ responds to eve enhancers, with MicroC showing preferential crosslinking of eve-gfp to the eve TAD and transgene homie interacting with both endogenous boundaries (strongest with homie).
results.evaluation: Claims C155-C159 show that reversing homie orientation switches both the functional response (Figure 5) and the physical interaction pattern (Figure 7C, 7D, 8B). The consistency between expression and MicroC data strongly supports the boundary-pairing model's prediction of orientation-dependent loop topology.

results.result: LhomieG and LeimohG transgenes show strong interactions between transgene and eve locus, with the reporter upstream of homie showing preferential interaction, and no evidence of the larger eveGa TAD predicted by loop extrusion.
results.evaluation: Claims C160-C164 confirm the pattern observed with the G-series transgenes in the opposite chromosomal orientation (Figure 6—figure supplements 1-2, Figure 8A-B). The absence of eveGa TAD despite reporter activation (C163) is particularly strong evidence against loop extrusion, though the poorer MicroC quality for LhomieG (noted in text) adds some uncertainty.

results.result: The orientation of homie within the transgene determines which reporter interacts with eve (independent of chromosomal orientation), while the transgene's chromosomal orientation affects how flanking sequences interact, consistent with different loop topologies (stem-loop vs circle-loop).
results.evaluation: Claims C165-C168 synthesize the key findings from all four transgenes. The separation of effects (homie orientation determines reporter activation; chromosomal orientation affects flanking interactions) is clearly demonstrated across the dataset and provides strong support for orientation-dependent boundary pairing generating different loop topologies.

results.result: The pairing properties of homie and nhomie are likely representative of most fly boundaries, as all tested boundaries show pairing activity, multimerized binding sites for generic boundary proteins mediate pairing with partner specificity, and many boundary proteins form dimers/multimers enabling physical linkage.
results.evaluation: Claims C170-C175 argue for the generalizability of the findings based on extensive prior literature. The evidence from multiple boundary systems (C171), multimerized binding sites (C172-C173), and protein biochemistry (C174) provides strong support that boundary pairing is a general mechanism, not unique to homie/nhomie.

results.result: Nearly 60 meta-loops identified by Mohana et al. show orientation-dependent boundary pairing interactions linking distant TADs, including the Lar meta-loop (head-to-head pairing, circle-loop) and beat IV meta-loop (head-to-tail pairing, stem-loop), with simpler single-contact-point interactions than the homie transgenes.
results.evaluation: Claims C176-C182 present additional examples of boundary pairing from the genome (Figure 9). The MicroC data clearly shows the predicted interaction patterns for both circle-loops (Lar) and stem-loops (beat IV), providing independent validation that boundary pairing with orientation-dependence occurs naturally at other loci.

results.result: Analysis of the eve neighborhood suggests circle-loops may be the predominant topology, as only eve TAD (and possibly TA) shows a clear stem-loop structure with volcano plume, while other TADs lack plumes and are overlaid by hierarchical LDC domains consistent with head-to-head pairing and partner switching.
results.evaluation: Claims C183-C187 propose that circle-loops predominate in the eve neighborhood based on the absence of volcano plumes in most TADs. While this interpretation is consistent with the boundary-pairing model, it remains somewhat speculative as the MicroC data alone cannot definitively distinguish between all possible configurations. The accompanying paper (Ke et al., 2024) may provide additional support.

results.result: The orientation of physical interactions bringing enhancers and promoters together determines transcriptional activation, and this topological constraint cannot be overcome by simply changing distances, as transcriptional efficiency is highly distance-dependent (continuous bursting at close range, reduced bursting at 6-9 kb).
results.evaluation: Claims C188-C193 discuss the functional implications of loop topology for gene regulation. The orientation-dependence is clearly demonstrated by the transgene experiments (C188), and the distance-dependence of transcriptional bursting is well-supported by cited live imaging studies (C190-C192), making the inference about topological constraints (C193) reasonable.

results.result: Long-distance regulatory interactions in vertebrates are likely subject to the same topological constraints as in flies.
results.evaluation: Claim C194 speculates about the generalizability to vertebrates. While the authors appropriately qualify this as speculation and note their studies don't directly address vertebrates, the claim remains uncertain without experimental evidence. The fundamental principles may be conserved, but vertebrate chromosomes have different organizational features (e.g., CTCF/cohesin-dependent TADs).

results.result: The authors conclude that their findings are incompatible with the loop-extrusion model and instead support a boundary-pairing mechanism for TAD formation in Drosophila, where boundary elements physically pair with their partners in an orientation-dependent manner.
results.evaluation: Multiple reviewers note that while the data support boundary-pairing, the authors did not experimentally deplete loop extruders to formally exclude their contribution. Reviewer 1 states 'an inability to deplete loop extruders formally leaves open a possible contribution of loop extrusion,' and Reviewer 2 emphasizes that 'loop extrusion and pairing are not mutually exclusive models' and that 'multiple smaller loops could bring together the two boundary elements, which are then held together by pairing proteins.' Reviewer 3 similarly notes 'they do not completely rule out additional models at play, including extrusion-based mechanisms.'

results.result: The authors claim that the absence of vertical and 45° crosslinking stripes in MicroC data is inconsistent with loop extrusion, as such stripes would be expected from loop extrusion intermediates captured by crosslinking.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 4 challenges the interpretation of stripe absence, stating 'In order to see stripes, a majority of the nuclei would need to undergo loop extrusion at the same rate, starting from exactly the same spots, and the loops would also have to be released and restarted at the same rate.' The reviewer requests experimental evidence from organisms known to undergo loop extrusion to validate that such stripes would actually appear. This critique questions whether the absence of stripes is truly diagnostic of the absence of loop extrusion.

results.result: MicroC analysis shows that the eve TAD is a stem-loop with a volcano plume, defined by nhomie and homie boundaries, while most neighboring TADs lack volcano plumes and are instead surrounded by LDC domains.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge the MicroC data showing the eve TAD structure or the presence/absence of volcano plumes in different TADs. The editor notes 'The evidence supporting boundary:boundary pairing as a determinant of 3D structures is compelling,' which implicitly accepts the structural characterization of TADs from MicroC data.

results.result: Transgene expression assays demonstrate that the orientation of the homie boundary determines which reporter (lacZ or gfp) is activated by eve enhancers, with GeimohL showing lacZ activation and GhomieL showing gfp activation, consistent with orientation-dependent boundary pairing.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 states 'The transgene expression assays are built upon prior knowledge of the enhancer activities' and 'Using 4 different orientations covers all combinations of the reporter genes and the boundary placement.' Reviewer 3 notes 'the transgenic experiments are extensive and elegant and fully support the authors' models.' The expression data are accepted as demonstrating orientation-dependent effects.

results.result: MicroC data from transgene lines show strong crosslinking between the transgene and eve locus, with the pattern of crosslinking correlating with reporter expression and demonstrating that transgene homie interacts with both endogenous homie and nhomie, with self-pairing interactions being strongest.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 confirms 'The 3D DNA contacts confirm that transgene expression correlates with the contacts.' The correlation between MicroC crosslinking patterns and reporter expression is not challenged by reviewers, supporting the claim that physical interactions mediate regulatory outcomes.

results.result: The orientation of homie in the transgene determines which reporter physically interacts with the eve TAD (independent of transgene chromosomal orientation), while the chromosomal orientation of the transgene impacts how flanking sequences interact with each other.
results.evaluation: This conclusion integrates the expression and MicroC data across all transgene orientations. Reviewer 2 notes the comprehensive coverage: 'Using 4 different orientations covers all combinations of the reporter genes and the boundary placement,' and the data supporting these orientation-dependent effects are not disputed.

results.result: The GhomieL transgene results demonstrate that boundary pairing can generate circle-loops (not just stem-loops), which is incompatible with loop extrusion since loop extrusion cannot generate circle-loops.
results.evaluation: While the expression data from GhomieL are accepted, the interpretation that this definitively rules out loop extrusion is questioned. Reviewer 2 notes that 'the imaging results seem to be consistent with both boundary:boundary interaction and loop extrusion stem looping,' and Reviewer 4 states 'most of this imaging data seems to support both loop extrusion and the boundary:boundary models.' The claim that circle-loops cannot be explained by any variant of loop extrusion is not fully accepted.

results.result: The minimal 367 bp homie fragment used in transgenes lacks the CTCF motif but contains binding sites for several other boundary proteins including BEAF, Zipic, Su(Hw), Pita, and Ibf2.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 4 raises a significant concern: 'The Homie region inserted in the transgene does not contain the CTCF motif. Can the authors elaborate on why they feel the orientation of Homie is important in its ability to function as a roadblock if the CTCF motif is not present? Trans-acting factors responsible for Homie function have not been identified and this point is not discussed in the manuscript.' This indicates uncertainty about the mechanistic basis for homie function.

results.result: Live imaging data from Chen et al. 2018 showed that in blastoderm embryos, the majority of nuclei (~80-85%) did not express the lacZ reporter and the transgene was distant from eve (~700 nM), while in expressing nuclei the transgene was closer (~330 nM) and remained in proximity for extended periods (~30 min).
results.evaluation: Reviewer 4 notes 'The authors appear to cite Chen et al., 2018 as a reference for the location of these transgenes being 700nM away in a majority of the nuclei. However, the exact transgenes in this manuscript do not appear to have been measured for distance. The authors could do this experiment and include expression measurements.' This indicates the cited distance measurements may not directly apply to the current transgenes.

results.result: The TADs between eve and hebe show hierarchical LDC (low density contact) domains that could arise from proximity of coiled circle-loop TADs leading to inter-TAD crosslinking, or from switching/combining pairing partners, rather than from cohesin breakthrough events.
results.evaluation: The observation of LDC domains is not disputed. The proposed mechanisms for generating these patterns in the boundary-pairing model are presented as alternatives to loop extrusion breakthrough, and reviewers do not challenge these specific mechanistic proposals for LDC domain formation.

results.result: The properties of homie and nhomie are likely representative of most fly boundaries, as all tested fly boundaries show pairing activity, multimerized binding sites for boundary proteins can mediate pairing with partner specificity, and many boundary proteins form dimers/multimers that could physically link boundaries.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 notes 'The authors essentially repeat many of their previous work and analyses,' which implicitly acknowledges the established nature of boundary pairing properties in flies. The generalization from homie/nhomie to other boundaries is supported by the cited literature and is not challenged by reviewers.

results.result: Analysis of meta-loops (including Lar and beat IV) shows that distant TADs are linked by orientation-dependent boundary pairing interactions, forming either circle-loops (head-to-head pairing) or stem-loops (head-to-tail pairing), with simpler single-contact-point interactions than the homie transgenes.
results.evaluation: The meta-loop analysis provides additional genomic examples of boundary pairing beyond the eve locus. Reviewers do not challenge these observations, and they serve as supporting evidence for the generality of boundary-pairing mechanisms in Drosophila.

results.result: Analysis of TAD organization in the eve neighborhood suggests that the predominant loop topology may be circle-loops rather than stem-loops, as most TADs lack volcano plumes at their apex.
results.evaluation: This interpretation of the MicroC data (absence of volcano plumes in most TADs) is not disputed by reviewers. However, Reviewer 3 raises a broader conceptual question: 'the authors' analyses do not distinguish between the formation and the maintenance of domains,' suggesting the static MicroC data may not fully capture dynamic processes.

results.result: The GlambdaL control transgene (lacking boundary elements) shows weak but detectable crosslinking with the eve locus, likely mediated by eve promoters in the transgene, but this low-level interaction is insufficient to drive reporter expression.
results.evaluation: The observation of weak interaction in the control is noted but not challenged by reviewers. This serves as a baseline for comparison with boundary-containing transgenes and demonstrates that boundary elements are required for functional regulatory interactions.

results.result: The orientation of physical interactions between enhancers and promoters determines transcriptional activation efficiency, and distance is a critical rate-limiting factor, as live imaging studies show that transcriptional burst frequency and amplitude decrease substantially with increasing enhancer-promoter distance (from continuous bursting at close range to infrequent bursts at 9 kb).
results.evaluation: These claims about distance-dependent transcriptional efficiency are supported by citations to published live imaging studies and are not challenged by reviewers. They provide mechanistic context for why topological organization matters for gene regulation.

comparisons.comparison: Both address the main conclusion (C10-C12, C169) that boundary-pairing drives TAD formation. OpenEval finds this SUPPORTED by multiple lines of evidence, while peer reviewers rate it UNCERTAIN, noting that loop extruders were not experimentally depleted and that the two models are not mutually exclusive.

Both discuss the absence of loop-extrusion signatures (stripes) in MicroC data (C86, C99, C103, C149-C151). OpenEval considers this SUPPORTED critical negative evidence against loop extrusion, while Reviewer 4 rates it UNCERTAIN, questioning whether stripes would actually appear even if loop extrusion occurred, requesting validation from organisms known to undergo loop extrusion.

Both address the eve TAD structure from MicroC data (C80-C83). OpenEval finds the stem-loop topology SUPPORTED, and peer reviewers also accept this structural characterization as SUPPORTED, with the editor noting the evidence for boundary pairing is compelling.

Both discuss orientation-dependent transgene expression patterns (C124-C126, C130-C141). OpenEval finds these SUPPORTED as critical tests distinguishing models, and peer reviewers also rate them SUPPORTED, with Reviewer 3 calling the transgenic experiments 'extensive and elegant.'

Both address correlation between MicroC interactions and functional activation (C145-C148, C152-C159). OpenEval finds this SUPPORTED, and peer reviewers agree (SUPPORTED), with Reviewer 2 confirming that '3D DNA contacts confirm that transgene expression correlates with the contacts.'

Both discuss the synthesis of findings across all transgene orientations (C165-C168). OpenEval finds this SUPPORTED, and peer reviewers also rate it SUPPORTED, noting the comprehensive coverage of all orientation combinations.
